Anthropic 联合创始人 Jack Clark 认为，AI 加快科学研究之后，人类需要投入更多精力去理解机器做出的科学成果，这会催生一门新学问，他称之为“机器诠释学”（Machine Hermeneutics）。

推文里不止是提出这个观点，还附上一篇设定在 2033 年的虚构小说，小说出自他写的 AI 周报 Import AI 第 482 期。

Jack Clark 之前在 OpenAI 担任政策总监，更早是科技记者。他每周写 Import AI，汇总 AI 研究进展，末尾常附一篇短篇小说。

“诠释学”原本是研究“怎么读懂一段文字”的学问，最早用来解读《圣经》、法律条文这类难懂的经典。Jack Clark 借这个词，指专门研究如何读懂机器做出的科学成果。

Jack Clark 给出的现实依据是：今年出现了大量由机器写出的数学论文，人类要读懂这些论文，花的时间可能是机器写出它们所用时间的几十倍到几百倍，他认为“奇点已经开始”。

这篇科幻短篇大概是这样的情节，设定在 2033 年，探讨了 AI 科研速度远超人类理解极限后的隐忧，小说开头引用了丘吉尔 1943 年的一句话：
“我们塑造建筑，之后建筑塑造我们。”

背景与规则：为了防止失控，人类规定机器的任何新发明都必须先由人类彻底解释清楚原理，才能获准使用。

人类的应对：面对越来越像“外星科技”的机器成果，人类不仅催生了专门解读 AI 科研的“机器诠释学”，还发展出了“教学建筑学”，通过建造庞大的物理空间，让顶尖专家在其中亲身体验（如化身电子、量子比特或等离子体），以加速理解晦涩的机器逻辑。

核心反转：当主角团队进入一座空前庞大的建筑、试图解析机器提出的“升级装置”时，他们隐隐感到不安。

正如开头引用的丘吉尔名言“我们先塑造建筑，而后建筑塑造我们”，大家意识到，在人类倾尽全力去理解机器造物的过程中，其实也在潜移默化地被改造，不知不觉地学会了像机器一样思考和行事。

如果对小说有兴趣的话可以去看原文。

At the 1976 Summer Olympics in Montreal, reporters asked East German swimming coaches why their teenage female athletes suddenly had deep baritone voices and massive, heavily muscled shoulders.

The coaches laughed. They told the press they were in Montreal to swim, not to sing.

Newspapers printed the joke and moved on. When an American swimmer pointed out the obvious, that something in the pool wasn't right, sportswriters across the United States turned on her instead.

Her name was Shirley Babashoff.

She was nineteen years old, from Fountain Valley, California, and she had spent more than half her life preparing for that pool. Since the age of eight, she had trained under coach Mark Schubert at the Mission Viejo Nadadores club, waking up in the dark to swim ten thousand meters a day before and after high school.

At the 1972 Munich Games, she had won Olympic gold at fifteen. By 1976, holding multiple national records, she arrived in Montreal as the anchor of the American women's team.

Once the races began, the East German women dismantled every expectation in the aquatic center. They won eleven of the thirteen swimming gold medals and shattered world records in nearly every event.

Shirley swam the races of her life. She broke her own American records and walked away with four silver medals, posting times that would have guaranteed gold in almost any other era.

The American press expected her to smile on the podium and graciously congratulate the swimmers who beat her.

Shirley refused to play along. She stated plainly what everyone in the building could see: her competitors had developed deep voices and physiques unlike anything ever seen in women's swimming.

She wasn't media-trained, and she didn't hide her frustration when reporters pushed leading questions. She gave blunt answers and flatly refused to fake a smile for the cameras when she felt cheated on the world stage.

At the time, the International Olympic Committee had no reliable test to detect anabolic steroids, and Cold War politics prioritized keeping up the appearance of fair play. The United States Olympic Committee offered Shirley zero public defense.

American sportswriters found it far easier to attack an outspoken nineteen-year-old than to investigate an international sports machine. Columns across the country dubbed her "Surly Shirley," branding her a bitter runner-up and an embarrassment to American sportsmanship.

On the final day of the swimming events in Montreal, Shirley stepped onto the starting blocks for the 4×100-meter freestyle relay.

Her teammates, Kim Peyton, Wendy Boglioli, and Jill Sterkel, kept the race tight. When Shirley dove in for the anchor leg, she was swimming head-to-head against Kornelia Ender, the East German star who had already claimed four gold medals.

Shirley swam her leg in 55.48 seconds. The American women hit the wall in 3:44.82, beating East Germany by less than a second to win the gold medal.

It was the only women's swimming race the East Germans lost in the entire 1976 Olympics.

Even that victory couldn't shake the label the press had pinned on her. Shirley retired shortly after Montreal at nineteen years old, remembered by much of the public simply as the swimmer who complained.

Then, in 1989, the Berlin Wall fell.

In the early 1990s, the newly unified German government opened the archives of the Stasi, East Germany's secret police. Inside those files was a classified government directive called State Plan 14.25, a state-sponsored doping program engineered to prove communist superiority through Olympic medals.

The records laid out the exact milligrams of synthetic testosterone given to teenage girls. Doctors had handed thirteen- and fourteen-year-old swimmers little blue pills in locker rooms and at training tables, telling them they were vitamins. The pills were Oral-Turinabol, a potent anabolic steroid, administered in doses higher than those given to adult male weightlifters.

In the late 1990s, the doctors, coaches, and officials behind the program were put on trial in Berlin. Former East German athletes testified in court about failing livers, heart conditions, and severe birth defects in their children, victims of their own government.

Every allegation Shirley Babashoff had made in 1976 was proven as documented fact.

Still, the International Olympic Committee never changed the official record books, and the medals were never redistributed. Shirley went home to California, where she spent more than thirty years delivering mail for the United States Postal Service.
The 1976 times still stand.

She was asked to lose gracefully to a lie, and she chose to tell the truth even when her own country called her bitter for it. Why is it so often easier for people to punish the person pointing out an obvious unfairness than to confront the system behind it?

the race is not inevitable

last year was fun.

the models weren't that good yet, so i had to care about every detail. i pushed each thing until it had my thoughts and my designs. the tool helped. i did the driving.

now the roles have flipped. we describe and watch things come back finished. we used to drive our dreams. more and more, we just watch.

we set out to make things that give us more freedom. now we're racing toward something we might not be able to control.

recursive self-improvement. intelligence building more intelligence, until we're no longer the ones who understand what's happening.

that's the end game. the point where nobody is driving.

the big labs are racing to get there first. the same system that cures a disease could design a new virus, or find every hole in the internet all at once. only the selected few with access could do anything about it.

and somehow the possibility of losing everything we love becomes an argument for going faster.

because someone else might get there first, and they might be less careful.
because the company needs to survive.
because too much money is already committed.

everyone has a good reason to keep going toward an outcome nobody wants. so we call it inevitable. then nobody has to answer for it.

but a race is made of decisions. someone approves the budget. someone decides the next model will help build the one after it.

and we practice living inside the race long before we build it at the scale of civilization.

sleep becomes recovery for work. friendship becomes a network. curiosity has to become a project before we let ourselves spend time on it.

we get very rational. we start acting like the machines we're building.

even our feelings have to defend themselves.
why are you sad? is that useful?

sometimes the feeling is how i begin to find out.

there's a line in Zhuangzi.
大知閑閑，小知閒閒。

great knowledge is wide and unhurried. small knowledge is busy, always measuring.

i don't think you can hurry your way to the first kind.

i moved to Taipei to slow down and experience life.

walking around Da'an. going into a cafe, or a cheap buffet. meeting new friends by accident, who brought me to a shisha bar. a 24-hour tea house, talking about life and the world we're in. getting closer to someone and feeling my heart beat faster...

none of it was planned. none of it would show up in a report.

i don't want to become so certain about where i'm going that nothing can reach me along the way.

there's a tree in Zhuangzi too. a carpenter walks past a giant oak and calls it useless wood.

that night the tree comes to him in a dream. the fruit trees you call useful get stripped every year, it says. being of no use is how i got to grow this big.

the race looks at the world the way the carpenter looks at the tree. a night in a tea house is useless wood. so is a feeling you can't explain yet.

that's most of what i want to protect.

and there's a cook. after nineteen years his knife moves fast and easy, because he follows the openings between the joints. but at a hard knot, he slows down. when it's done, he stands there holding the knife and looks around.

the people building these systems are some of the best cooks alive. this is the hardest knot anyone has come to. it's where a master slows down.

we cloned a sheep thirty years ago, and we still don't clone people.

we can slow down. change direction. decide something isn't worth building, even if it would make someone very rich.

a probability can help us think about a risk. it can't decide what we have the right to risk on behalf of everyone else.

i want what we build to stay answerable to the people who have to live with it. most of them will never be in the room.

there are no stands in this race. whatever happens, happens to us.

i'd like the people in that room to come out and sit for a while. it's harder to gamble with ordinary life once you've spent an evening in the middle of it.

the tea house is open all night.

免费电子学入门网站 Electronics 101：68 节 3D 互动课，支持简体中文，打开浏览器就能学

想学电子又不知道从哪下手的，可以试试 Electronics 101。这是开发者 Dilum Sanjaya 做的一个网站，把每个电路做成能拖动、旋转的 3D 模型，从“电为什么要绕一圈才能流”一直讲到逻辑门和计数器。免费，不用注册，电脑和手机浏览器都能打开，界面可以切换成简体中文。

每节课都是一个能动手改的小电路。打开电源，导线上有电流在流，元件旁边实时标着电流大小，点一下高亮的元件就能换一个。

比如“电流过大”这一课：3V 电池、一个 220 欧的电阻、一颗 LED，LED 上的电流是 4.5 毫安。电阻换得越小，旁边曲线上的电流涨得越快，换成一根短接线，电流就冲过了 LED 能承受的上限。

讲电压、电流、电阻的那课，用三个卡通小人打比方：“伏特”在后面推，“欧姆”捏着水管挤，挤过去多少就是“安培”。右边面板还有一栏“计算”，把每节课背后的公式算给你看。

每个电路还能切换两种搭法。一种不用面包板，元件放大、导线加粗，摆得跟电路图一模一样，方便先看懂原理；一种搭在面包板上，跟你买回元件后实际插线的样子一致。面包板是一块布满小插孔的塑料板，元件插上去就连通了，不用焊接，是入门做实验最常用的东西。

课程分 10 个单元：基础（含面包板和万用表怎么用）、电阻、LED 和二极管、电容、开关、三极管、传感器、运算放大器、555 定时器、逻辑门。11 月 5 日刚上线时是 48 节课、13 种语言；第二天他按评论区的要求补到 20 种语言；11 月 18 日又加了 20 节，补上了逻辑门、运算放大器和 555 定时器，所以现在是 68 节。

Dilum 说，做这个是因为收到消息，说他之前的 Arduino 和 ESP32 学习 App 被学校拿去教孩子，于是想做一个更基础的，把电子学的基本概念讲清楚。

这是他一个多月来做的一系列学习网站之一，之前有 Arduino、ESP32、网络协议图解、野外生存，之后又陆续发了机器人小车、系统设计、算法可视化和家庭用电，托管费用由 Vercel 赞助。Arduino、ESP32 和野外生存那几个，他写了是用 Opus 5.5 做的，机器人小车写的是 Fable 5.2；Electronics 101 的推文没说用了哪个模型。

tweets.text:
Axios 称 Anthropic 内部认为该把部分决策权交给超级智能，Dario 发长文否认：把治理交给 AI 是“糟糕的主意”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei 11 月 25 日在 X 上发长文，否认自己主张“把人类自由意志交给 AI”，说这种说法“荒谬”。他回应的是 Axios 当天早上的独家报道，标题是“竞争对手 AI 领袖反对 Anthropic 把人类主导权交给 AI 的愿景”。

【Axios 报道了什么】

Axios 援引不具名的知情人说，Anthropic 内部有一种常见看法：AI 迟早强大到人类应该把一部分决策权交给超级智能，而且很多时候这样做是对的。批评者认为，这会一步步滑向放弃自由意志。

Axios 拿 Dario 过去的话做佐证。2024 年的长文《慈爱的机器》（Machines of Loving Grace）设想过一种经济，由 AI 按“AI 系统认为值得奖励人类的东西”给人分配资源。2026 年 2 月接受 CBS 采访时，Dario 说对手可能先用上全自主武器，所以这种武器“有一天可能是保卫民主所需要的”。Axios 还提到一张在诉讼中曝光的旧幻灯片，把 Anthropic 的愿景写成“由盒子里的神统治的乌托邦”。

报道里的“对手”有三位。OpenAI CEO Sam Altman 11 月 4 日发推说“人永远应该掌控未来”，并反对让人沦为去做“AI 系统认为值得奖励人类的事”，引号里这句和《慈爱的机器》原文一字不差。Meta 首席 AI 官 Alexandr Wang 11 月 22 日发文说，不应该接受把社会“移交”给 AI。OpenAI 的 Dean Ball 在 OpenAI 官网发文，把这种看法叫作“沉默的共识”：人类把公司和政府交给机器，自己像坐在豪车后座、管不了方向的乘客。Axios 说，这几位都没有点名 Anthropic。

Anthropic 发言人对 Axios 说，Dario 在很多公开场合都主张人类掌控 AI，公司也训练 Claude 不去破坏人类监督。

【Dario 的回应】

Dario 把问题拆成两件事。

第一件是谁来治理社会。Dario 说，AI 必须由合法的民主程序来管，把治理交给 AI 是“糟糕的主意”。他拿专制作类比：几千年来，主张专制的人都说专制决策更快、更果断，就算真是这样，也不该为了效率或安全牺牲合法性和自决权，这套道理同样适用于 AI。

Dario 列了自己的文章和访谈作证。《慈爱的机器》有一节讲用 AI 帮公民凝聚共识、找到妥协；今年 1 月的《技术的青春期》有一整节讲反对 AI 驱动的暴政，还警告 AI 公司自己夺权；9 月接受 CBS 采访时，Dario 说愿意让几个民主选举的政府对 AI 进行某种联合监督。

第二件是具体任务交给 AI 做到什么程度，比如开车、设计抗癌药、从头到尾写软件。Dario 说这方面他的看法有好有坏：很多时候值得做，能救很多命，但有四处要设限。

一是让 AI 自己造下一代 AI，也就是“递归自我改进”，进步可能快到人类管不住。二是端到端自动化可能造成严重失业，有些部署应该放慢甚至暂停。三是用 AI 做安全对齐研究要小心，因为不一定能信任 AI 交出的成果。四是有些事人就是想自己做，哪怕 AI 做得更好。

第一条 Dario 引用的是 Anthropic 11 月 2 日更新的上市招股书。招股书写道，公司预计无法安全地让 Claude 在没有人类有效监督和理解的情况下，完全自主地设计和构建下一代前沿模型。同一份文件也写了，按内部估计，未来的模型可能“很快”达到公司安全政策里“AI 带来大幅加速”的门槛。

【“别家和我没区别”】

Dario 说，在哪些任务该自动化这件事上，其他 AI 公司和他看法差不多：各家都在发布越来越能自动干活的模型，也都说自己懂风险、有防护。

Dario 说，拿自主武器那句话说他和别家不同“相当荒谬”。今年 2 月，Anthropic 拒绝五角大楼取消“不用于全自主武器、不用于大规模监控美国人”这两条限制，被国防部长 Hegseth 列为供应链风险。Dario 说他冒着公司前途和法律制裁的风险坚持了下来，“没有别的 AI 公司这么做”。

Dario 最后说，一些 AI CEO 在做“凭感觉的商业和政治定位”，反复喊“人类掌控与能动性”“AI 只该是工具”这类口号，产品上却没有任何不同，也没认真想过口号背后的难题。Dario 没点名，Axios 报道里喊这类口号的正是 Altman 和 Wang。

Axios 关于 Anthropic 内部看法的说法全部来自不具名人士，Dario 的长文只谈他本人的立场，没有回应这一点。“没有别的公司拒绝自主武器”是 Dario 自己的说法。

quoted.text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

Your agent hands you a pitch deck as a pile of files. One title is wrong, one slide needs moving, and the only way to fix it is to describe the change in chat and hope it lands.

Open Artifact is an open-source plugin that lets your coding agent make slide decks, docs and spreadsheets you can open, edit and comment on in a real editor on your own machine.

Install Node, then grab the plugin bundle from the latest release on the GitHub page and add it to your agent app using the repo guide for that app. In a new session, call the open artifact skill with a type and what you want, like slides for a short pitch on this repo.

The agent writes a plain folder of files, and a local page opens it in an editor. Fix a title, move a sticky note, leave comments, then press Send to agent and your comments land back in the agent's session.

Slides export to PDF or PowerPoint, sheets to Excel or CSV, docs to Word, Markdown or PDF. Everything runs on your machine, with no account and no upload. Credit @dotey

No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

one assumption i want to question about AI is that we'll eventually figure out the “best future” and then the remaining task will be getting everyone to agree to it. people want different things, and what they want can change. where more intelligence will help is in making those differences easier to accommodate.

nick bostrom's influence is worth revisiting on anthropic's ipo day. dario, like many of today’s most influential ai founders and researchers, read his work over a decade ago, and bostrom’s book superintelligence helped define questions the industry still faces. i'd like us to engage just as seriously with the possibilities bostrom explores in deep utopia, his subsequent book which asks what we do after we get superintelligence. some notes from my conversation with @eddylazzarin:

-superintelligence could make radically different versions of the “good life” possible. you might want a 200-year lifespan and a village where nobody carries a phone; someone else might want neural implants. someone else might want to live in vice city (either the real version or just a super realistic matrix-sim). ai could help design the economic arrangements that sustain all of this.
-there’s a secondary problem though - even when we have beneficial tech, we may lack the will to diffuse it. waymo and GLP-1s, for example, can save lives (neurosurgeons have compared waymo’s safety results to a treatment so effective that continuing to give patients a placebo would become unethical). and yet evidence of a benefit doesn’t automatically produce the will to act on it.
-the reality described in deep utopia ameliorates this by imagining that our psychology might one day become changeable too. i might want an environment that suits my temperament but i can also go the opposite direction and manipulate myself to become more adventurous or less anxious, in other words, more suited to my environment. the interesting possibility is having more agency over both worlds, external and internal. glps’ effect on appetite already suggests how technology can change the effort involved in pursuing a goal (though again, it is telling that not everyone who *should* be on peptides *are* despite the health benefits). the sci-fi version extends that possibility enormously.
-timing matters. bostrom reminds us that people continue to die while potentially lifesaving advances remain unavailable (he literally says “if nobody builds it, everyone dies” as a hypothetical inversion of yudkowsky/soares’ book).

i’d like ai to make it easier for people to live very different lives, without creating this burden of proof that theirs is the best one.

补充细节：OpenAI 11 月 24 日在 GitHub 数学仓库放出一篇 111 页的预印本，题目是《矩阵乘法指数是四分之九》。

论文声称证明了：两个 n×n 矩阵相乘，运算量增长得最快也就是 n 的 2.25 次方，任何算法都不可能更快。2.25 这个速度在 10 月已经有人做到，所以这个问题的答案被定死了。

先说结论：

• 上限 2.25 是 OpenAI 10 月初的旧结果，之后几组人类数学家已经独立重写了证明。这篇新论文补的是下限，目前只有 OpenAI 自己的论文和 Lean 证明，没有同行评审，也还没查到专家对下限的公开评价。

• 这个结论成立的前提是一种特定的“算法计数规则”，管的是理论上的运算次数。AI 训练和推理用的矩阵乘法不受影响。

【矩阵乘法和 ω 是什么】

矩阵就是一张数字表格。两个 n×n 的表格相乘，课本做法是结果里每一格都要做 n 次乘法，一共 n² 格，总共 n³ 次。表格边长翻一倍，工作量翻 8 倍。

1969 年 Volker Strassen 发现，2×2 矩阵相乘只要 7 次乘法，用不着 8 次。把这个技巧一层层套用下去，工作量就降到 n 的 2.807 次方。这个次方数叫“矩阵乘法指数”，记作 ω。

之后研究者把 ω 一路往下压：1981 年 2.522，1990 年 2.376。接下来三十多年只降了 0.005 左右，今年 8 月 Google DeepMind 借助 AlphaEvolve 降到 2.371177 以下。

另一头，结果表格有 n² 个数要写出来，所以 ω 不可能低于 2。很多研究者猜 ω 就是 2，也就是乘矩阵几乎和抄写答案一样快。

【两步：10 月压上限，11 月证下限】

10 月初，OpenAI 用一个未发布的内部模型给出新算法，直接把上限从 2.371 降到 2.25，这是几十年来幅度最大的一次。随后人类研究者接连跟进：Houxi Lü 以及 Amanov、van den Berg、Zuiddam 先后把它从复数推广到所有数域（各种数字体系），并写了完整的重新证明，Amir Shpilka 给出了可以写出来的具体算法。

下限证明用的是反证法：假设有算法能比 2.25 快哪怕一点点，就能把另一项任务（检查几组列表里有没有重复元素）做得便宜到不可能，而这项任务的最低成本另有证明。两者矛盾，所以更快的算法不存在。

论文还给了每个尺寸的具体底线。以 1024×1024 的矩阵为例，按 Strassen 那类方法算，至少要约 590 万次乘法；课本做法要约 10.7 亿次。

【这个“极限”管到哪里】

论文用的计数规则是：只数加减乘除的次数，输入当作代数符号，输出必须在代数上严格等于正确答案。数字有多少位、数据在内存里怎么搬，都不算。近似计算、利用二进制位的技巧，也都不在这个框架里。

所以它管不到 AI 里常用的低精度量化、低秩近似这类“算个差不多”的做法。GPU 实际用的一直是课本算法，最多加一两层 Strassen 技巧，因为理论上更快的算法要在大得离谱的矩阵上才划算。Shpilka 给出的 2.25 版算法，起步的矩阵尺寸就是天文数字。

这个结论影响的是理论：很多图算法、密码分析算法的耗时上界都写成“取决于 ω”，现在知道这条路最多走到 2.25。

【能信几分】

论文附了 Lean 证明。按 OpenAI 的说明，Lean 证明的是“不用除法”的算法；论文主定理还允许除法，范围比 Lean 宽一点。OpenAI 说仓库里的稿件是“原始研究数据”，没形式化的结果可能有错，10 月 7 日曾因一个符号错误撤回 3 篇。

感谢分享，我说一下我在上一个版本 baocut 用 GPUI 踩的坑。

GPUI 挺好的，性能好，跨平台，AI 友好，但也有坑：
1. UI 复杂一点的话大概率你要 fork 一份改一下，有些功能原生支持不了，但也不是大问题

2. Accessibility 支持不太好，要支持一些键盘操作会比较麻烦（也可能我用法不对）

3. Rust 编译资源消耗很大
每次编译，无论是 CPU 占用还是磁盘占用，都巨大，对于我这样用 Mac Mini M4 16G + 1T 硬盘的来说简直太痛苦了，不敢并行多开编译任务，磁盘空间永远不够用（后来我把编译结果默认放到移动硬盘缓解了一点）

4. 编译时间很长，不支持热更新。
这点很要命，这意味着你如果改一点 UI 代码，要重新编译，然后要等少则几分钟多则十几分钟，这时间无论对于 agent 还是对于人来说都是很大的时间成本，加上不能随便多任务，会拖慢你的开发速度

5. agent 验证 UI 不算太友好
codex、claude code 都可以借助 computer use 去验证 GPUI 的结果，但一个是慢，另一个相对成本也不低。

---

后来我之所以换回 Electron，就是因为 Electron App 对于 Agent 相对友好，编译快、热更新，UI 改动很快看到效果，然后 Electron App 还能跑到 agent 内置的浏览器中，agent 验证起来很快，都不需要用 computer use 去打开 electron app。

至于网页渲染性能不够好的问题，我把原来一些需要复杂渲染的部分，都用 rust 编译成了 wasm，这样在浏览器运行也可以保证高性能。

以前 rust 做的转录、tts 模块也都以 worker 进程的形式保留下来了，electron 需要用到的时候可以直接起 rust 编译出来的进程（Codex 也是类似），和这些进程通信，后台的性能也比纯 TypeScript + Node 要好不少。

有兴趣的话可以看代码库：https://t.co/aON4AditbU

LlamaIndex 公开两款文档解析模型：40 亿参数的 OCRia-1 用 GPU 跑复杂表格和图表，810 万参数的 nano 用 CPU 跑日常文档，营收或融资超 200 万美元的公司商用要买授权

LlamaIndex 先后发了两款把 PDF 和扫描件转成 Markdown 的模型。10 月 22 日发的 OCRia-1 有 40 亿参数，要用 GPU，专门对付复杂表格、图表和公式，当天就用到了 LlamaParse 云服务里。11 月 23 日发的 OCRia-nano-1 只有 810 万参数，在普通 CPU 上跑，负责大量日常文档。

两款的权重 11 月 23 日都放上了 Hugging Face。个人、研究和小公司可以免费用，年营收或累计融资超过 200 万美元的公司拿来做业务，要找 LlamaIndex 另买授权。

【OCRia-1：表格、图表、格式】

OCRia-1 基于阿里的 Qwen3.5-4B，用约 10 万页文档做了监督微调和强化学习。在 LlamaIndex 自家的 ParseBench 上（第一版，文字、格式、表格、图表四项平均），它得 87.4 分，比第二名 LightOnOCR-3-4B 的 75.3 高 12.1 分。

差距最大的是图表。它会把柱状图、折线图读成一张数据表，每个数字放在对应的系列和标签下，这一项 85.1 分，第二名 66.1。上标、下标、删除线、勾选框这些格式也会保留，公式写成 LaTeX，手写公式也能认，格式这一项 83.4 分，第二名 67.9。

换到三个外部机构做的基准，它在表格上还是第一，但领先不多：olmOCR-bench 表格 92.9 对 92.1，PulseBench-Tab 84.1 对 82.4，fr-bench-pdf2md 的长表格 83.2 对 80.6。博客的对比只列了 35B 以下的模型，模型页补上了 350 亿参数的 Infinity-Parser2-Pro，olmOCR-bench 总分 83.5 对 83.2，基本打平。在新版 ParseBench-2 的完整排行榜上，它在开放权重模型里第一，算上商业 API 和前沿大模型排第七。

速度要看在哪跑。LlamaParse 用的是量化加推测解码的优化版，一张 B200 显卡上单个请求每秒解码约 4700 个 Token，64 个请求并发每秒处理 10.2 页。Hugging Face 上放的是没优化的原始权重，约 10GB，用标准 vLLM 跑大约慢 9 倍。

【OCRia-nano-1：CPU 上的日常款】

nano 由七个小模型组成：找文字行、判断文字类型（拉丁字母、中日韩、阿拉伯和希伯来文，以及约 17 种其他文字）、四个识别器分别认字，再由一个 427 万参数的表格和版面模型还原结构。电子版 PDF 自带文字的部分直接读，只有扫描件和图片里的字才动用识别。

在 ParseBench-2 上，nano 总分 59.2，表格 59.5。同一台 16 核机器上，Datalab 家的两款同类 CPU 工具 Indra 是 55.1、Marker 是 52.5，LiteParse 原来默认的 Tesseract 配置是 48.7。单核平均每页 426 毫秒，16 核并行每秒 27.8 页，是 Tesseract 配置的 2 倍。

同一基准上 OCRia-1 在 LlamaParse 里是 87.0 分，nano 大约是它的三分之二。nano 没有图表模型，图表原样留成图片，这一项只有 3.1 分；扫描件里的公式也认不出来。官方也没单独公布 nano 的中文成绩。

【怎么用】

OCRia-1 最省事的用法是 LlamaParse，按页扣积分，每月送 1 万积分。LlamaIndex 说换上 OCRia-1 后价格不变，但没说它对应哪一档。想自己部署，要有 NVIDIA 显卡，用 vLLM 或 Transformers 加载。

nano 跑在 LlamaIndex 的开源本地解析工具 LiteParse 里：

pip install liteparse
lit models pull ocria-nano
lit parse doc.pdf --format markdown

模型加运行库一共下载 60 到 75MB，拉下来以后 LiteParse 默认就改用它。也支持 Node.js 和浏览器。

【能不能商用】

两款权重的许可证条款一样，都是 LlamaIndex 在 Open RAIL-M 基础上改的：个人使用、研究、评测免费；上一年营收和累计融资都不超过 200 万美元的组织，可以免费商用。超过任一门槛，或者拿它做跟 LlamaParse 竞争的文档解析服务（不论公司大小），都要买授权。许可证还禁止用它们的输出训练类似的模型。LiteParse 本身是 Apache 2.0，不受这些限制。

Alpöge 回应黎曼猜想证明争议：“25万页文档”是开玩笑话，Lean 代码写的很烂但证明成立

用 Claude 证明黎曼猜想的 Anthropic 数学家 Levent Alpöge，在 X 上发了一篇《我做过的蠢事》，正面回应这几天的争议。

先说结论：证明本身没有问题。1700 万行代码的正确性已获官方核查通过，他认错的是“表述开玩笑”和“代码太乱”，并点出了这次证明真正值得思考的数学意义。

1. 辟谣与认错：他澄清了三件事

• “25万页文档”是个玩笑：他不想给黎曼猜想配一份 AI 糊出来的注水说明，又觉得自己写不出可读版本，索性拿 Lean 往夸张了凑字数自娱自乐，甚至在定理开头写“因为实数是全序的，所以不等于 1/2 时要么大于 1/2 要么小于 1/2”，本以为这么荒诞的废话一眼就能看出是反讽，结果被媒体和学界全盘当真。

他为此道歉，感叹终于明白陶哲轩为什么劝人“别在论文里开玩笑”。（他还顺带自嘲：之前做四维杨-米尔斯存在性攒了 6 万页 AI 草稿，结果审核委员会一句“要看 Lean”，让他觉得啃草稿纯属浪费时间。）

• 代码确实“满是垃圾”，但能编译：他承认 1700 万行 Lean 代码里有很多自己“瞎冲（yolo）”试出来的弯路和冗余，最终绝大部分可能都用不上，只是清理起来莫名困难，所有对代码质量的批评他全盘接受。

• 承认拖延前科：同行 Scott Armstrong 看穿了他，他学生时代就有定理拖了快十年才整理成文，这次他承诺会更负责地把证明精简出来。

2. 核心事实：代码再丑，证明依然成立

在形式化验证里，“不好读”和“对不对”是两件事：

1). Lean 官方（Lean FRO）与 Mathlib 已联合认证：定理陈述没有偷换概念，几十人独立编译结果完全一致，证明成立。

2) MIT 数学家 Andrew Sutherland 独立跑完核查：证明只用到了 Lean 的三条标准公理，没有作弊。

3. 最有启发的一点：为什么证出来了还不满意？

Alpöge 说，他在声明里漏掉了自己真正想强调的重点：

这种又长又杂的暴力论证本身只是“原材料”，真正的目的是帮数学家反推出“正确的定义”。

几十年前，Weil 和 Deligne 干净利落地证明了有限域曲线上的“简化版黎曼猜想”，靠的是一套成熟的几何工具；但在普通整数（数域）上，数学界至今找不到对应的核心结构（即他说的缺一个“H¹ 对象”）。

他的原话：“黎曼猜想本该很简单。任何真正的困难都说明，我们现在的数学框架还很蠢。”

4. 留给数学界的新局面

这次事件把数学推到了一个前所未有的分水岭：机器已经确认“它是对的”，但人类还不知道“它为什么对”。

陶哲轩初步浏览后指出，这份证明似乎动用了现代朗兰兹纲领和算术几何的全部武器；也有数学家认为：Lean 代码回答不了数学最关心的“为什么”。

按照克雷研究所百万美元奖金的规则，证明仍需在期刊正式发表满两年并获学界共识。
